items.action: The muleta, emblem of Seixal and Barreiro, trawled sideways: the net (tartaranha) was cast windward and the boat drifted across wind and current.
items.conditions: drifting broadside to wind and current

items.action: Baldaque da Silva described the muleta's sails as arranged to balance forces by wind and current direction, with two long poles (botalós) fore and aft to set sails and tie net wings.
Author argues sideways trawling existed in France with a boat and net both called tartane; the net is documented in Portugal as tartaranha from the 15th century.
The word muleta appeared in the 16th century as a generic name for various vessels.
Some Frenchmen introduced a new tartane model to Portugal, fishing with the tartaranha net; the Seixal/Barreiro muleta is therefore no earlier than the 17th century.
Muleta name is traced to Latin for mullet; in France mulet was also a river boat. Maurolico's 1543 manuscript mentions mullet fishing.
Many mullet species were abundant in Portugal, entering rivers in huge shoals; they suited salting, drying and smoking and were among the most fished and traded.
items.conditions: salting, drying and smoking preservation

items.action: Italians Lourenço Berardi and Giovanni Morosini took part in the mullet fishery in Portugal.
Seville ordinance required a pound of albur (mullet) to sell at the same price as a pound of mutton, confirming an older one.
King João I banned fishing shad and mullet for anyone not leasing the fishery; the 1433 Cortes asked for the order's revocation.
items.conditions: fishing allowed only to those holding a lease

items.action: Mullet fishing was important enough to justify voyages to Terra Alta, Arguim and Cabo Branco on Africa's west coast.
Lisbon's Casa do Pescado collected the sisa tax on salted mullet from Terra Alta.
The Casa de Bragança won a judgment against the Count of Atouguia over the tithe on mullet from Arguim castle and coast.
items.who: Casa de Bragança; conde de Atouguia

items.action: Royal letter of 6 Nov 1487 ordered that fish caught by Lisbon's deep-sea fishermen be exempt from the fixed sale price (taxa).
items.conditions: taxa is the sale price set by the almotacé

items.action: Second royal letter of 28 Nov 1487: deep-sea fishermen sell without price-setting or weighing; price rules apply only to river fishermen, chinchas and tartaranhas.
items.who: pescadores do alto; pescadores do rio, das chinchas e tartaranhas

items.action: In Lisbon, deep-sea fishing (pesca do alto) meant fishing from the bar outward, not at a fixed distance from the coast.
The chincha net dominated Lisbon fishing, so fishermen were called linheiros (line and hook) or chincheiros (any kind of net: gillnet, trawl, encircling).
items.gear: linha e aparelhos de anzol; redes chincha, de emalhar, arrasto, cerco

items.action: João Brandão reported 15 chinchas on the river, each with eight men, fishing by turns either as enviadas (carrying fish) or with tartaranha nets.
items.conditions: enviadas carry fish to unloading places

items.action: In Alfama, linheiros and chincheiros had separate brotherhoods in different churches: Espírito Santo at São Miguel, and Nossa Senhora dos Remédios at the Remédios chapel.
Linheiros fishing beyond the bar were called pescadores do alto or altieiros; chincheiros do alto fished the open sea with nets.
By royal order the Lisbon council gathered tartaranha nets at the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios in Alfama to check mesh size.
items.conditions: inspection of malhagem
items.place: ermida de Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, Alfama

items.action: Council ordinance set minimum mesh for chinchorros and other nets and required baked-clay balls instead of lead weights to avoid disturbing the bottom and catching young fish.
items.conditions: protect spawn and juvenile fish; clay lighter than lead
items.gear: chinchorro (beach seine), bolas de barro cozido

items.action: In 1610 the council justified mesh rules because dragging chinchorros along the bottom took roe and young fish, causing their loss.
Royal decree confirmed a Cascais council ordinance banning tartaranha barcas from sailing between São Julião and Cabo da Roca, because of harm to Cascais fishermen.
items.conditions: ordinance of 12 March 1592, alvará of 11 July 1592
items.place: São Julião to Cabo da Roca
items.who: câmara de Cascais; pescadores de Cascais

items.action: The boat fishing with the tartaranha net was variously named chincha, barca, barco, tartaranha or chinchorro across documents.
The name muleta appeared in the 16th century for river boats; Inquisition records of 1550 mention it in Lisbon, and Fernando Oliveira noted santarém boats renamed from cervilhas to muletas.
Moors chased Portuguese swimmers in two zavras, built like muletas, after the loss of Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué castle.
items.place: castelo de Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué

items.action: The 1572 Regimento dos Barqueiros regulated cargo and passenger transport on the Tagus, compiling norms of different dates, and covered muletas and other river craft.
Batéis crossing from Lisbon to Almada may carry at most 8 people under paragraph 19, though paragraph 61 permits 12.
Larger barcas and caravelões must carry a compass; muletas and small batéis are exempt.
According to the author, all muletas were cargo boats and none were used for fishing.
Paragraph 21: from 1 October to end of March, skippers and boatmen of lateen-rigged boats must carry carregadeiras on the yards so sails can be lowered quickly, avoiding disasters.
items.boat: barca, caravelão, muleta, batel pequeno de vela latina
items.conditions: winter season; disasters when sails cannot be lowered
items.gear: carregadeiras nas vergas; roldana na cabeça do mastro
items.period: 1 October to end of March, each year

items.action: Cerveira de Aguilar explains the mast head (calcês) has two sheaves on large vessels, through which halyards (ostagas) pass to hoist and lower yards; small vessels may have one.
items.conditions: two sheaves on large vessels, one on small

numbers.what: sheaves on calcês of large vessels

items.action: Aguilar lists four ways of rigging halyards, including the calcês, the cachola with sheaves under the crosspieces, and blocks on iron straps under a wooden cepo on the mast head.
items.conditions: cachola used when no calcês
items.gear: calcês, cacholas, cepos, blocks, iron straps

items.action: Jerónimo Osório describes the lateen caravel as having no crow's nests, with oblique yards hanging from a sling below the mast head.
items.period: same era as Aguilar (c. 1640 era, 16th c

items.action: Article 36 of the 1572 boatmen's regulation: muletas crossing the river must carry only a round sail for safety, with a yard no longer than the hull, and always a foresail.
items.conditions: muletas cannot tack 'por dentro' like caravelões and large barcas, risking sail falling on the mast

items.action: Muletas sailing the river without people or cargo may use a lateen or round sail, but must never sail without ballast.
items.conditions: only when empty of people and cargo

items.action: Author explains tacking 'dar por davante' means turning the bow through the wind; muletas with lateen sails could not pass the sail across because it fell on the mast.
items.conditions: alternative was wearing ('virar em roda'), passing the stern through the wind

items.action: Hernâni Amaral Xavier proposes caravelões and large barcas hoisted lateen sails between shrouds and mast, muletas outside the shrouds; the author calls this very risky.

The regulation implies two masts with round sails, main and foresail, whereas known illustrations show muletas with a very long yard and large sail. Pinto Basto notes flat bottom and stone-and-lime ballast.
items.conditions: flat bottom, wide mouth give stability

items.action: A Lisbon council consultation attached a copy of a bylaw repeating the rule that muletas crossing the river use only round sails, showing the regulation partly endured.
items.conditions: muletas cannot tack 'por dentro'

items.action: The 1572 regulation uses vague terms: larger vessels are barcas and caravelões, smaller ones muletas and batéis.
Article 41 sets the maximum freight for boatmen of Abrantes, Tancos, Punhete and Santarém sailing from Lisbon by muleta; beyond Santarém price is agreed with customers.
items.conditions: for the largest muleta, ten moios or more; above Santarém freight by agreement

numbers.what: maximum freight Lisbon to Santarém, largest muleta

items.who: barqueiros of Abrantes, Tancos, Punhete, Santarém

items.action: No boat or bateira may carry a person or goods meant for the scheduled service boat until the Arraiz da Molleta has been paid his freight, unless the service boat has already left; penalty applies.
items.conditions: Exception only after the carreira boat has departed; offender pays the Arrais what he earned plus a
items.location: A Muleta e a Tartaranha, Alverca posturas
items.who: Arraiz da Molleta; boatmen of Alverca

items.action: Boatmen bound to the carreira each serve the town one week in turn, going to Lisbon every day; on night runs they must stay aboard to take charge of passengers' baggage until the boat leaves the esteiro.
items.conditions: One week per boatman by custom; night departures require staying aboard
items.location: A Muleta e a Tartaranha, Alverca posturas

items.action: Each week one boat or bateira was designated to run the scheduled service to Lisbon and became the 'molleta' of the carreira for that week.
items.conditions: Rotation weekly
items.location: A Muleta e a Tartaranha, Alverca posturas

items.action: Smaller muletas carrying goods were allowed to settle by agreement with parties, provided the sum did not reach 800 réis (fragment of a freight rule near Santarém).
items.conditions: Agreement with the parties, limited to under the stated amount

items.action: Santarém boatmen petitioned that the river was heavily silted, so large caravelões and barcas no longer came, only smaller batéis and muletas.
items.conditions: River silting

items.action: Nicolau de Oliveira noted many small boats called moletas in Lisbon that fished continually in the river.
Freight rates for carrying goods from Lisbon to Alcochete: large barca cost more than a muleta or similar vessel.
items.conditions: Rate depends on vessel size

items.action: The regulation on fish tithes of the Casa de Bragança mentions 'river sardine muletas', showing muletas used for sardine fishing.
Engineer Leonardo Turriano's opinion foresaw Lisbon muletas going to the Guadalquivir and Seville, likening them to shallow-draft flat boats of Flanders and Italy.
items.conditions: Flat boats drawing little water; canal to suit two masted boats

numbers.what: canal width at low water surface

items.who: Leonardo Turriano, engenheiro mayor de Portugal

items.action: Padre Manuel Godinho described Persian Gulf terradas and terranquis as like Tagus muletas but wider and keelless, low bow, very high stern, one mast, lateen sail, oars, no deck.
items.conditions: Sail taken off the yard whenever the wind changes; a canopy with a bed sits on the stern
items.gear: lateen sail, oars, rudder steered by cords

items.action: Other sources compare terradas to Alcochete barcas or large boats fought from by 25 to 30 men, too vague to identify the type.
items.conditions: Vague information

items.action: Corsairs are described using narrow, light, hence unsafe vessels called terradas, sailing with very large lateral (lateen) sails and rowing with twelve or fifteen oars per side.
The tartaranha was the first trawl net to be banned, in the 15th century; the ban stayed rigorous on paper but was tolerated after fishermen's pleas until the 20th century.
items.conditions: strictly forbidden yet tolerated after fishermen's appeals

items.action: The term muleta first appears for a boat fishing with the tartaranha in documents of 1634 and 1645; muletas were smaller than barcas.
Lisbon council reported excessive tartaranha fishing, saying no other fishing method was used any more, whether in barcas or in the smaller muletas.
An almotacé saw two muletas with tartaranha nets near Belém Tower and requested soldiers; the soldiers disobeyed his orders and resisted.
The king ordered a Lisbon councillor to proclaim a ban on tartaranha boats and nets in every river and sea of the kingdom, with severe penalties, including keeping nets at home.
items.conditions: penalties: flogging, fines and exile; applied to everyone regardless of status
items.who: o rei, vereador da câmara de Lisboa

items.action: The king ordered an inquiry into whether fish stocks had grown after one year of the ban on tartaranhas.
Lisbon council found tartaranhas harmful in the river because tight dragged nets take young fish and roe; they should fish only in open months, with the legal mesh and light gear.
items.conditions: closed months March, April, May (spawning); free fishing allowed below São Julião tower
items.gear: clay balls instead of lead weights, cork floats, regulated mesh

items.action: The king agreed and authorised tartaranha fishing outside the bar.
items.place: fora da barra, torre de São Julião

items.action: Baked clay balls are lighter than lead and press less on the seabed.
Tartaranha fishermen supplied fish to Lisbon and acted as bar pilots assisting India ships, royal fleets and merchant ships.
items.boat: naus da Índia, armadas, naus mercantes
items.who: pescadores das tartaranhas, chincheiros do alto

items.action: A royal charter confirmed permission for tartaranhas outside the bar, in response to representations from the fishermen, also called pilots of the bar.
The first regulation for Lisbon bar pilotage admitted as pilots only those with ten years of continuous experience on offshore fishing boats.
items.boat: barcos de pescaria de barra em fora
items.conditions: ten years' successive practice required

items.action: An English parliamentary fleet blockaded the Tagus near the bar and on 13 June seized Portuguese fishing boats, after a royalist fleet took refuge in Lisbon.
items.conditions: blockade from late March to late September 1650

items.action: On 24 June King João IV wrote to the Algarve governor and the Count of Ericeira that the English had seized tartanas that were fishing.

numbers.what: tartanas fishing near the bar, at least

items.action: Fishing with the tartaranha net was done from boats that the sources first typed as tartanas; earlier they were called barca, barco, tartaranha, chincha or chinchorro.
The term muleta with rede tartaranha already appeared in 1634 and 1645, but only as a generic designation.
A Lisbon council ordinance allowed muletas fishing with chinchorros, being smaller than chinchas, to use lead weights on the net's two sides, but clay balls along the whole cuada.
items.conditions: clay balls kept on the cuada because it drags the young fish and destroys the roe; bulky nets on the
items.gear: chinchorro nets, clay balls, lead weights

items.action: The smaller mesh gauge set earlier applied only to tartaranhas, not to chinchas and chinchorros, which needed mesh able to catch sardine, their main purpose.
A trawl net consists mainly of a bag and two sleeves (mãos), which hold the bag and channel fish into it; the cuada is the bag's narrow-meshed end.
items.gear: rede de arrasto, saco, mangas, cuada

items.action: An anonymous 17th-century author proposed stretching an iron chain across the Tagus to block a seaborne attack on Lisbon, using old boats or muletas as floats.

numbers.what: old boats or muletas needed as buoys

items.action: Beam trawling with a boat and net both called tartana is of Provençal French origin, documented from 1301; it appeared in Catalonia and Mallorca in the late 14th century.
From the late 16th century Provençal fishermen, especially from Martigues, migrated to Ligurian, Tuscan and Lazio waters with the tartana, called martingana.
A document at Pesaro mentions the new tartana fishing method, spread by French fishermen in several parts of the world.
The 'several parts of the world' meant a restricted Mediterranean zone between Catalonia and the Adriatic and, in the Atlantic, only Portugal.
A boat made for use as a tartana was sold at Pesaro.
items.boat: barca fatta ad uso di tartana

items.action: A flat-bottomed fishing boat, the nascara, was sold at Chioggia for tartana use; its inventory listed two tartana nets. Italian boats were adapted for beam trawling.
During João IV's reign some Frenchmen sought to introduce a new model of tartaranha with a vessel also of a new type.
A king used the word tartana (vessel) together with tartaranha (net) in a letter, after deep-sea line-and-hook fishermen had opposed a French fishing proposal and the king refused it.
items.gear: tartaranha (net); linhas e aparelhos de anzol

items.action: Two Frenchmen again asked to introduce the new tartaranha net and vessel; the king passed the request to Lisbon's city senate, which advised against it and the king refused.
items.conditions: Senate said the new nets were more harmful, with smaller mesh and a much larger bag circumference
items.who: two Frenchmen; senado da câmara de Lisboa; the king

items.action: The senate argued French tartanas resembled the launches of Moorish corsairs who raided the coast, so fishermen might mistake them and confront them by accident.
items.conditions: Fishermen would find it hard to tell the vessels apart
items.place: coast of Portugal; Estreito de Gibraltar
items.who: senado da câmara de Lisboa; Moorish corsairs

items.action: Estevam da Luz asked leave to build four large vessels at his own expense to fish far out at sea; the king granted a four-year exclusive licence.
items.conditions: Nobody else could arm a similar vessel for four years
items.who: Estevam da Luz, resident of Lisboa; the king

items.action: The Espírito Santo brotherhood, representing deep-sea fishermen, again opposed the petition, but the senate called the invention very useful and favoured it.
items.who: confraria do Espírito Santo; pescadores do alto; senado

items.action: The senate's favourable opinion ran for three years, after which natives were free to use the invention; the king approved, limiting each vessel to two Frenchmen.
items.conditions: Each vessel could carry no more than two Frenchmen

items.action: Spanish author Veitia Linage described tartanas as lateen-sailed Levantine-crewed vessels suited to fishing at sea, some sent to the Indies; foreign sailors were needed for the sails.
items.conditions: Spaniards did not understand the rigging; three or four foreign sailors had to be allowed

items.action: The tartana had lateen sails for navigating and extra sails for trawl fishing, which required foreign (French) sailors.
items.gear: lateen sails; complementary sails for trawling

items.action: The oldest known illustration of the French fishing tartana appears in an album by Jean Jouve of Marseilles.

The earliest illustration of the muleta, not yet mentioned by Portuguese authors, appears in Gueroult du Pas's album published in Paris, which also shows the tartana for fishing off Provence and Italy.
items.place: Paris; coasts of Provença and Itália

items.action: Figure 2 shows three tartanas: one with a single mast and lateen sail, one with an extra triangular sail on a pole, one fully rigged for beam trawling.
items.gear: mast, yard, lateen sail, triangular sail, pole; trawl rig

items.action: The muleta is shown under way without trawl rigging, with a forward-leaning mast, lateen sail, forward boom with a square sail, raised inward-curving ends and a leeboard on each quarter.
items.gear: lateen sail; botaló with quadrangular sail (cevadeira); two leeboards

items.action: This is the first documentation of the leeboard in Portugal; it appears on other vessels only later, in the Caderno de todos os barcos do Tejo.
The muleta has three features never seen on French fishing tartanas: inward-curving bow and stern, forward-leaning mast, and leeboard. The 1710 album shows leeboards only on Atlantic boats.
items.conditions: Mediterranean boats had no leeboards

items.action: The leeboard reduces leeward drift and prevents capsizing; it is needed only on flat or nearly flat-bottomed lateen-rigged boats, not on round-rigged ones, and is lowered on one side.
items.conditions: Flat-bottomed boats with lateen rig

items.action: Two theories exist on the leeboard's origin in Europe; one holds it is Chinese and reached Holland in the late 16th century.

Dutch leeboard (zwaard) described as three planks stacked and cut in a shoe-sole shape; Dutch and English fishing and trading vessels of the 17th-18th centuries used it, some with four boards, two per side.
items.boat: Dutch and English fishing and trading vessels
items.who: Dutch authorities; Dutch and English fishing and trading vessels

items.action: Per Nicolas Aubin, leeboard dimensions followed set proportions: length twice the vessel's depth, width half the length, thickness twice the hull planking.

numbers.what: leeboard length relative to vessel depth
leeboard width relative to its length
leeboard thickness relative to hull planking

items.action: Leeboards were made slightly wider for rivers and shallow water, slightly longer and narrower for deep, rough water, and narrower still for ocean-going ships; many exceptions existed.
items.conditions: little water under the keel makes boats turn more easily
items.place: rivers, shallow waters, deep waters, high seas

items.action: The muleta's leeboard took several different shapes, while the Dutch yacht (jachten) sailing the Indian Ocean had a very large one.

The muleta used its leeward leeboard while sailing to reduce leeway, one board on each side; Portuguese authors name it variously (tábua de bolina, pau de borda, pá de borda, esparrela de deriva, tábua de abatimento).
items.conditions: sailing with the wind; leeward side
items.gear: tábua de bolina / pau de borda
items.who: Portuguese authors (Tengarrinha Pires, Castello Branco, Lixa Filgueiras, Baldaqu

items.action: Duhamel Du Monceau published an engraving of the Portuguese muleta, shaped like a gondola with raised bow and stern, rowers placed amidships.
The 1772 muleta engraving shows a steeply raked mid-mast with lateen sail, a triangular bow sail, net ends tied to two booms, a huge rudder worked by tackles and a transverse tiller.
items.conditions: under sail, not rigged for trawling
items.gear: lateen sail, triangular sail, net, booms, rudder with tackles, leeboards

items.action: The muleta's bow carried a crest of iron points, described as a strong iron bar nailed to the bow's outer face to protect it, as other European boats did at quays.
items.conditions: protection when boats hit the quay, often head-on
items.gear: iron bar with pointed nail heads
items.who: Manuel Leitão, Ferdinando Simões, A. Marques da Silva

items.action: Duhamel Du Monceau says muletas trawled sideways like Mediterranean tartanas, fishing sardines at night between Peniche and Setúbal, usually hauling nets ashore; the author calls this wrong.
items.conditions: at night

items.action: The author states that the muleta with tartaranha net was not meant for sardine fishing and fished beyond the Tagus and the sea between Cabo da Roca and Cabo Espichel; 1758 parish records mention Setúbal muletas.
items.place: Tagus; Cabo da Roca to Cabo Espichel; Setúbal

items.action: Royal order banned use of tartaranha boats and nets for fishing in any river or sea of the kingdom, hinting they were already on the Sado.
items.place: every river and sea of the kingdom

items.action: Prince regent's decree banned dragging nets (tarrafas, chinchorros, mugeiras, tartaranhas) in the Lisbon and Setúbal rivers and within five leagues of their mouths, citing harm to fish breeding.
items.conditions: to protect fish breeding; applies at sea and on beaches
items.place: rios de Lisboa e Setúbal, and five leagues from their mouths

items.action: The muleta fished with the tartaranha net in the Tagus and Sado estuaries and at sea between Cabo da Roca and Setúbal.
items.place: Tejo and Sado estuaries; sea between Cabo da Roca and Setúbal

items.action: The muleta in the 1785 Caderno has a short mast raked forward, lateen sail, triangular jib, two booms, arched bow with iron spikes, receding stern, two leeboards.
items.gear: lateen sail, triangular bow sail, leeboards, metal bow band with iron spikes

items.action: Barco de Riba Tejo, thought to be the cargo variant of the muleta, closely resembles it.
The Batel de Pesca shares the muleta's forward-raked mast, sails, metal bow band with iron spikes and leeboards.
items.gear: leeboards, metal bow band with iron spikes

items.action: An engraving by João Pedroso published in 1866 showed a muleta very like the 1785 one; a model was also built that year.
Muleta designs of 1710 and 1772 had features absent from French fishing tartanas: raised ends, forward-raked mast, leeboards, tackle-operated rudder, iron-spike crest on bow.
items.gear: leeboards, rudder worked by tackles, iron spikes

items.action: Writers described the muleta hull as broad and flat-bottomed with a rounded, raised bow, comparing it to a Norman naveta or Greek ship.
items.who: Baldaque da Silva; Octávio Lixa Filgueiras

items.action: Origin of the muleta is uncertain; in 17th-century Italy local boats were adapted to trawl sideways with tartana nets, and this may have happened in Portugal.

numbers.what: first known illustration of French fishing tartana

items.action: The 1572 boatmen's regulation states only that muleta yards were very long.
Father Manuel Godinho compared Persian Gulf terradas to Tagus muletas, though the terradas differ, with low bow and very high stern.
items.gear: lateen sail, rudder steered by cords

items.action: To ease sideways trawling and use shallow draught, muleta and Barco de Riba Tejo had flat or inward-curving bottoms so the keel sat tangent.
items.conditions: shallow draught; sideways trawling

items.action: Trawling with two boats dragging a large bagged net astern developed in the Mediterranean, called parelha, bou or chalut; in France it was called 'aux boeufs'.
The bou reached the Gulf of Cádiz, brought by Valencians, and spread across southern Spain as far as Ayamonte.
Bou nets were highly productive because their small mesh formed a 'wall' once the doubled, heavily weighted lead lines touched bottom; xávega and 'arte' nets were similar.
items.gear: small-mesh net with double heavy leads

items.action: The Spanish king ordered the Catalan bou banned in Galicia without banning xávega; the two were judged similar, bou hauling aboard and xávega to the beach.
The Archbishop of Thessalonica reported Valencians fitting out bou boats in the Algarve, and Portuguese imitating them with similar boats and nets, depleting fish stocks.
items.gear: Mão, Copo, Quada, Saco, Chinchorro, Nova Arte nets

numbers.what: Valencian bou boats in the Algarve

items.action: A letter from the viscount of Vila Nova de Cerveira reported similar transgressions by fishermen of the northern provinces, Sesimbra and Setúbal.
items.who: viscount of Vila Nova de Cerveira

items.action: Mão, saco (copo) and cuada are the parts of a trawl net; chinchorro is a trawl net; Nova Arte is the Algarve xávega and the west coast 'arte'.
A document criticised Lisbon's city senate for tolerating many three-mesh-order trawl nets that catch all young fish; it counted the boats fishing this way.
items.gear: nets of three mesh orders (mão, copo, saco)
items.place: Barreiro, Seixal, Arrentela, Paio Pires, Sacavém, river, Costa

items.action: The 12 saveiros off the Costa de Caparica fished with xávegas; the other boats likely used chinchorros and/or tartaranhas.
The muleta (tartaranha net) and other trawls like bou were strictly forbidden yet tolerated after fishermen's pleas.
items.conditions: officially prohibited but tolerated
items.location: 14. As Limitações à Pesca com a Muleta e o Bou

items.action: A Portugal–Spain fishing reciprocity convention barred bou, parelha, chalut and similar trawls, and Portuguese muletas, within 12 miles of the other's coast; confirmed in 1885.
A survey found Portuguese customarily fished in Spanish waters using gear prohibited in Spain.
The tartana, used for fishing and cargo, is documented at Sanlúcar de Barrameda since the 18th century; a c.1910-1920 photo shows a muleta-like one-mast lateen rig.
items.gear: inclined mast, yard, triangular lateen sail

items.action: From the late 19th century, smaller boats (batel, bote, bateira) also trawled with the tartaranha net; the name muleta was often applied loosely to any boat fishing with it.
Baldaque da Silva recorded that by 1891 only one muleta remained.
Tartaranha nets continued to be tolerated until their final extinction around 1920.
items.conditions: tolerated until extinction

items.action: Brito Aranha reported muletas crewed by 6, 10, 12 or 16 men, depending on the fishing intended and the boat's size.
items.conditions: crew depends on type of fishing and size

items.action: Seixal muletas had larger crews, and the biggest were about 20 metres long.
The smaller tartaranha botes were 12 m long, with a beam of 3.60 m, depth of 1.50 m and a crew of 15.
The cargo muleta was practically the Barco de Riba Tejo, and the two are hard to tell apart.
items.boat: muleta de carga, Barco de Riba Tejo

items.action: Rascasço made 79 drawings in three notebooks, Costumes das nossas embarcações, including the Alhandra cargo muleta.
Muletas and rascas ventured beyond the bar, sometimes many miles out, seeking cargo from abundant ocean fisheries.
Muletas did coastal trading to the Algarve, bringing its products to the Tagus or exchanging them at Moroccan ports.
A muleta could be rigged as a yacht (iate) with two or three masts for some commercial commission.
A two-masted fishing muleta appears in a Pierre Ozanne engraving, probably from the late 18th century.
The 19th-century muleta had an enormous yard and huge lateen sail, which became dangerous in strong wind.
items.conditions: strong wind

items.action: Furling the sail: crew climbed the yard, first reducing sail area with brails, then rolling the cloth by hand and securing it.
items.conditions: dangerous work; men climbed in reverse order of weight

items.action: Unlike the Mediterranean, Portugal did not shrink the yard or switch to square sails; its large lateen sails impressed foreign authors.
Duhamel Du Monceau said the French tartana could trawl with four to ten sails, though known images show fewer.
Baldaque da Silva described the late-19th-century Portuguese muleta carrying 9 or 10 sails: main sail, two varredoura triangles aft, and six or seven small sails on stays.
items.gear: vela grande, varredoura de cima, varredoura de baixo, toldos, muletins, cozinhei

items.action: The tartaranha bote, last boat to fish with this net, had somewhat different sails.
The muleta carries a very large number of small sails, said to set it apart from boats anywhere in the world; the sail plan is shown for the tartaranha boat.
William Henry Smyth reported that the muleta often set as many as twenty different sails, high and low, puzzling unfamiliar seamen.
The Marquis de Folin described at least twenty, sometimes more, small sails of all shapes, giving a fantastic look; the rig was already old-fashioned.
items.conditions: fishermen later learned to trawl with fewer sails

items.action: The tartaranha net bag was cone-shaped, as shown in the sail plan figure of the tartaranha boat.
In the late 19th century the conical net was replaced by a rectangular net made of seams, following an opinion of the Comissão Central de Pescarias.
A decree replaced the conical tartaranha net with the rectangular seamed net.
Rebelo says muletas paid out cable so the net reached the bottom, hauls lasted hours and the net was hauled by hand; the author doubts this.
items.conditions: author argues a windlass or other device would have been used

items.action: Comparable boats used hoisting gear for nets: the lancha poveira had a windlass, and Dutch fishing ships show nets rigged to cables going to the masthead.
The author corrects other writers: the beach-hauled net described at Costa de Caparica is the xávega, not the tartaranha net.
Other fishing methods of muletas are undocumented but were probably gillnets, handlines, multi-hook lines and possibly stern or pair trawling.
Bluteau defined muleta as a Lisbon river boat for fishing or carrying goods, with side boards he took for rudders; the author says they are leeboards.
Bluteau defined the tartaranha as a fishing boat with a lateen sail and two long poles from bow and stern, used on the Tagus.
Bluteau described the varredoura net as very fine-meshed, used by muletas to catch even the smallest fish; the author resolves the confusion of terms.
Moraes Silva's dictionary defined muleta as a small Tagus fishing boat and muletim as its small sail.
Per Moraes Silva, boats from Lisbon to Belém could carry only one sail plus a muletim.
Vieira's dictionary described the muleta as a small fishing boat launched outside the Tagus bar, with the muletim as its only sail.
French dictionaries from 1687 called the mulet a medium Portuguese ship with three lateen-rigged masts; the author thinks they confused it with the tartane.
items.conditions: known engravings show the muleta with one mast

items.action: English dictionaries from 1701 called the single-masted fishing boat muleta a 'bean-cod', supposedly from its resemblance; the term later covered small lateen-rigged boats of the Tagus estuary.
Small lateen-sail boats sailed constantly past Lisbon in any wind or tide, as described by Edward Clarke in a letter.
items.conditions: any wind or tide

items.action: A 1730 description of Lisbon reports a huge quantity of fish unloaded by caravelles and muletes.
Each cod-fishing ship carried several small boats that left at dawn daily from the fishing ground and returned at dusk with the catch.
items.boat: small boats carried by bacalhoeiro ships
items.conditions: daily, dawn to dusk

items.action: Around 1875 the small boats carried by cod ships became dories; before that they were larger and heavier.

numbers.what: approximate year of change to dories

items.action: Falconer's 1769 dictionary describes the bean-cod as a small fishing or pilot boat with a sharp, curved, iron-plated stem and large lateen sail good for sailing to windward.
items.conditions: sails well to windward
items.gear: iron-plated stem with bolts; large lateen sail

items.action: Muleta crews also performed pilotage services.
A 1794 English work compared the one-masted Portuguese bean-cod to the French tartan, as a fishing or pilot boat.
In 1892 the marquis de Folin held that all boats around Lisbon derived from the muleta, extending the name to all Portuguese craft.
Willaumez described two models: the one-masted mulette or moulète, and the mulet with two or three forward-leaning masts and lateen sails.
The pinque closely resembles the mulet, differing mainly in its vertical main mast.
The muleta was known to French and English writers; its drag-style rig set it apart from boats elsewhere, and it resembled the French tartane.
The muleta served as the boat of the pilots of the Lisbon bar, in the main Portuguese port where sailors from everywhere passed.
The caravela, long a generic name for small and medium ships and boats, stopped being mentioned in the second half of the 18th century; the muleta took its place.
Caravels from Galicia sailed to Cabo Branco to fish sharks and mullets, which were dried in the sun like cod from Newfoundland.
items.cargo: chiens de mer (sharks), mullets, other fish
items.conditions: fish dried in the sun

items.action: Beam trawling is thought to have originated in Provence, using a boat and a net both called tartane.
Earliest document mentioning the tartane dates from 1301; the net was soon judged harmful because narrow meshes dragged along the bottom destroyed small fish and young.
items.conditions: narrow meshes dragging on the bottom

items.action: Fishermen of the Seneschalty of Beaucaire protested against tartane fishermen for destroying fish; the tartanas were banned from Easter to All Saints' Day.
items.conditions: ban from Easter to All Saints' Day
items.who: pescadors de las tartanas; fishermen of Beaucaire

items.action: The tartane net was called tartaranha in Portugal, a bird of prey name; tartane means falcon in modern Provençal. It was the first trawl net banned in Portugal.
Royal letter responded to Lisbon officials' complaints about tartaranha fishermen using fine meshes that caught young fish; it ordered no fine nets beyond previous custom.
items.conditions: fish shortage blamed on young fish being caught
items.who: vereadores, procurador and procuradores dos mesteres of Lisbon; tartaranha fishe

items.action: The tartaranha targeted flatfish living on sand (azevias, linguados, solhas) but also caught other species from seabed to surface.
The net had cork floats on the upper line and weights (lead, clay or stones) below, near the bag that trapped fish; floats and weights set pressure on the seabed.
items.conditions: pressure on seabed depends on floats and weights
items.gear: cork floats, lead, clay or stone weights, bag

items.action: Duhamel Du Monceau described French fishermen adjusting corks, lead and stones to the seabed; on sand they added more lead to force flatfish up to swim.
items.conditions: depends on nature of seabed; sand bottom is hard and firm

items.action: Another rigging used much cork on the top line and only light stones on the bottom, spaced fathom by fathom, so the net floats mid-water.
items.conditions: net floats mid-water or lightly touches bottom

items.action: Despite the ban, each Lent some tartaranhas in the Tagus estuary fished azevias and linguados to supply the king in Madrid.
items.cargo: azevias and linguados for the king's Lenten table
items.conditions: tartaranhas banned; Lent, a strict fasting period

items.action: Lisbon's câmara stated the yearly fishing of azevias and linguados for His Majesty's Lenten meals.
A possibly 14th-century summary of goods exempt from or subject to royal and municipal duties in Lisbon lists fish branches, possibly including the tartaranha.
items.cargo: pescado da messa, azevias e linguados, chinchas
items.conditions: part of the text is illegible

title: Pedrosa, A Muleta e a Tartaranha (sec. XV-XX)
